newsitem.title: USA: Clinton urges UPS, Teamsters to reach deal,end strike.
newsitem.headline: Clinton urges UPS, Teamsters to reach deal,end strike.

text.p: President Bill Clinton on Sunday urged the Teamsters union and United Parcel Service to redouble efforts to reach an agreement and end a 2-week-old strike that has paralyzed package deliveries by companies throughout the United States.
"It's clear that they're making progress," Clinton told reporters before boarding his helicopter to leave for vacation on Martha's Vineyard.

"This strike is beginning to hurt not only the company but its employees and the people who depend on it and I think they ought to redouble their efforts to settle the strike and they ought to do it today," the president said.
Deputy White House counsel Bruce Lindsey told reporters travelling with Clinton that he believed the two sides would either reach a settlement on Sunday or break off negotiations.

Teamsters President Ron Carey said earlier on Sunday that marathon talks with UPS negotiators had made progress for the first time since negotitators hunkered down in a Washington hotel at the request of Labor Secretary Alexis Herman on Thursday morning.

"There has been some movement," Carey said in explaining why he believed he was right not to put the company's previous so-called "last and final" offer to his 185,000 members for a vote as UPS executives had been urging.

"We are talking about the issues and that to me is progress -- trying to see if we can find some areas of agreement and the talks are moving along," Carey said on the NBC television program, "Meet the Press."
Company and union negotiators continued meeting on Sunday at a hotel across the street from the International Brotherhood of Teamsters headquarters.
Asked if the union planned to stay at the bargaining table until a deal was reached, Carey said, "Absolutely."

UPS Chairman James Kelly, appearing on the same program, also sounded an optimistic, though cautious, note, saying that negotiators were discussing "dozens and dozens of issues" but it was unclear when an agreement could be reached.
"The fact that we're continuing to talk is encouraging," Kelly said, reiterating that the company would use replacement workers only as a last resort.

"We've been at make or break points a number of times before," Kelly told CNN later on Sunday. "Perhaps we're at another one right now." When asked if there was a chance that a settlement might be reached by midnight Sunday, Kelly responded, "anything is possible."
The two sides have been meeting in face-to-face sessions, with federal mediators and with Herman since Thursday morning, taking only a few brief sleep breaks along the way.
Herman, who was credited by both sides with helping to keep the talks moving, is scheduled to fly to Los Angeles on Monday for a speaking engagement.

The walkout by drivers, loaders and sorters on Aug. 4 has crippled the nation's largest package delivery firm to the tune of an estimated $300 million a week in lost revenues and has cost UPS more than a half-billion dollars so far.
Kelly said the strike could take a lasting bite out of the company's 80 percent market share, which would translate into fewer jobs when the dispute was settled.
UPS competitors, including the U.S. Postal Service, have rushed to try to fill the void. But many small businesses are feeling the pinch of being unable have their goods delivered.
UPS officials this week responded to a request by the Federal Reserve Board, sending officials there a detailed analysis of the strike's impact on the company and the economy.

An Oklahoma lawyer announced on Saturday that he filed a federal lawsuit against UPS on behalf of a number of small and medium-sized companies, charging the shipper with breach of contract and negligence and seeking at least $75,000, the minimum required in federal court.
Carey has announced plans for rallies in 30 U.S. cities on Thursday to drum up support for the strike. He said unions representing UPS workers in several European countries also planned job actions.
Buoyed by opinion polls showing the strikers winning the public relations battle, Carey has stuck to his theme that UPS convert more part-time jobs into higher paying full-time jobs.
For its part, UPS has been seeking the withdrawal of its pension plan from its current multi-employer plan so it can set up a plan solely for Teamster members at UPS.
The strikers were getting help from other unions, but were finding it tough to live on $55-a-week strike benefits.
Clinton has been resisting calls by UPS and some business groups to seek an injunction under the Taft-Hartley Act that would temporarily halt the strike.
